clue.text: Definitely wearing a suit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an idiom for 'emphatically, without doubt'
second meaning, read literally: dressed in one of the four card suits

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing a suit' pictures office clothes, but the suit is one of the four in a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiomatic phrase means to a great degree or emphatically, and literally names a card suit.

clue.text: What terse youngster might say to his parents, honestly!

parts.words: What terse youngster might say to his parents
parts.note: surface reading: a curt child speaking to mum and dad; setter's reading: a clipped child would say 'I, your child, am not (joking)', missing words out

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a telegraphic sentence, the phrase is a child saying 'I, kid, (am) not ...'; read normally it is an assurance of sincerity.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom used to stress that one is being truthful, so it means honestly.

clue.text: Took a chance in Sweden and embezzled

parts.note: S is the international vehicle code for Sweden
to peculate is to embezzle public funds

explanation.surface: A fraudster gambled while in Stockholm and stole money.
explanation.definitionFit: To speculate is to invest riskily in the hope of profit, i.e. to gamble.

clue.text: Saw lawyer in time

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, held by the surrounding word

parts.note: an age is a period of time
a District Attorney, the US prosecutor

explanation.surface: Someone spotted their attorney just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see; it is the noun meaning a saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or proverb, so it is a synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Plant manufactured panel heaters

indicators.note: something manufactured is made up from raw materials, so the letters are made into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A factory producing panel heaters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a factory alongside 'manufactured', but it is a growing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant's ear is the common name of colocasia and similar large-leaved species, so it is an example of a plant.

clue.text: Look like getting point, holding City

parts.note: 'as' and 'like' both mean in the manner of

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so the next word goes within the pair before it

parts.note: PT is the standard abbreviation for point
EC is the postcode for the City of London

explanation.surface: Someone resembles a person scoring a point while keeping hold of a City team.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcodes begin EC.
explanation.definitionFit: A look is an appearance or facet, which is a synonym for the answer as a noun.

clue.text: Hit (by mistake) a journalist

parts.note: a slip is a small error
per means for each, a, as in 'ten pounds a head'
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: Someone accidentally struck a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket makes 'by mistake' look like an aside, but it holds a piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To be slippered is to be beaten with a slipper, an old school punishment, so it means hit.

clue.text: Lippy, could you say, trying to be cool?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, cryptic: a lip is an edge, so something lippy might be called this
second meaning: deliberately daring or unconventional

explanation.walkthrough: Lippy usually means cheeky, but here it is read as 'having a lip', and a lip is the rim or edge of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes art or fashion that is provocative and trendy, so it fits trying to look cool.

clue.text: 'What I just said is rubbish,' Hunt originally admitted

indicators.note: to be admitted is to be let in, so the first piece goes inside the second

parts.note: tat is cheap, worthless stuff

indicators.note: originally points to the origin or start of the word, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of Hunt

explanation.surface: A politician named Hunt concedes that his earlier remark was nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunt suggests the British politician Jeremy Hunt, but only his initial is used.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points back to something just mentioned, as in 'that is true'.

clue.text: Repeats article cost (throwing away money)

indicators.note: throwing something away discards it, so those letters are dropped from the joined words

parts.note: an item is an article, a single thing
rates are charges, what something costs
M is the abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: A shopping note complaining that the price of an article was wasteful.
explanation.walkthrough: The joined words ITEM RATES lose their M to leave ITERATES.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to do or say again, a synonym for repeating.

clue.text: Through with old lady virtually — might this help?

indicators.note: virtually means almost entirely, so the word is used all but its final letter

parts.note: via means by way of, through
a gran is a grandmother, an old lady

explanation.surface: A cheeky aside about getting through an evening with an elderly woman, wondering what might help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virtually' means almost all of it, so the last letter of the grandmother word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: The drug treats erectile dysfunction, so the question hints at what an ageing partner might rely on.

clue.text: Pompous Conservative objects to this red claptrap

parts.note: stuff means things, objects

indicators.note: claptrap is nonsense, so the preceding words are turned into a jumble

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A self-important Tory protests against this left-wing nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Objects' looks like a verb meaning protests; it is the noun meaning things.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a pompous, stuffy and conventional person, typically a conservative one.

clue.text: Song's poor? Utter phooey!

indicators.note: poor here means badly made or in bad shape, so the letters that follow are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dismissive review: is this tune bad? Complete nonsense!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' sits with 'Song' in the surface, but it works on the two words after it. The answer is a Cole Porter number from 1934.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of a famous Cole Porter show tune, so it is an example of a song.

clue.text: Engine's shot, as bad driver might have said earlier

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing an engine type

indicators.text: as bad driver might have said
indicators.note: this points to a word spoken by a wayward golfer, so its sound rather than its spelling counts

parts.note: the golfer's shouted warning after a wayward drive
a stroke is a shot in golf

explanation.surface: A car's engine is ruined, as a reckless motorist might have warned before.
explanation.walkthrough: The driver is a golfer whose drive goes astray, not a motorist; 'earlier' places the shout before the shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-stroke engine is a common type of internal combustion motor, so the word describes an engine.

clue.text: Yank paid seller for something a bit ropey

indicators.note: as a verb to yank is to pull sharply, so the letters are wrenched into new positions

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An American bought a shoddy item from a vendor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American; as a verb it means to wrench, so the letters are jerked about. Ropey is British for poor quality.
explanation.definitionFit: An espadrille is a canvas shoe with a sole of plaited rope, so it is partly made of rope.

clue.text: Country's reportedly in order

indicators.note: reportedly means as told by word of mouth, so the answer is a spoken match for the phrase

parts.note: the United Kingdom's, said quickly

explanation.surface: A news item saying the nation is apparently in good shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A ukase was an edict of the Russian tsar, so it is a decree or command.

clue.text: Bishop's Stortford originally involved in great work round China

indicators.note: being involved in something means being caught up within it, so one piece is set inside another

parts.note: an epic is a grand literary work

indicators.note: originally refers to the beginning, so only the opening letter of the town is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Stortford
O is round in shape
china is rhyming slang: china plate means mate

explanation.surface: A grand work about Bishop's Stortford, a Hertfordshire town, taking in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bishop's' runs into Stortford as a place name, but it is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Episcopal means relating to a bishop or bishops, so it matches the possessive form.

clue.text: 'Foul, ref!' Unai's getting worked up over nothing

indicators.note: getting worked up means becoming agitated, and agitated letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A football manager, Unai Emery, is shouting at the referee over a non-incident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foul' looks like part of the touchline shout, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Foul can mean wicked or villainous, which is what the answer describes.

clue.text: What some airlines do with tickets is concerning affair

definitions.text: What some airlines do with tickets

parts.note: over can mean about, concerning
an issue is a matter, an affair

explanation.surface: A complaint that airline ticketing practice is a worrying business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' reads as worrying in the surface; here it means about.
explanation.definitionFit: Airlines often sell more seats than a plane holds, betting on no-shows, which is to issue too many.

clue.text: Russian woman foiled a raid

indicators.note: a foiled plan is thrown out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A spy story in which a woman from Moscow thwarts an attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foiled' reads as thwarted, but a foiled plan is thrown out of shape, so the letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Daria is a common Russian female first name, so it is an example of a Russian woman.

clue.text: Vegas gambler not good — finally gets a warning

parts.note: slang for poor quality

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the final letter of gets
a hooter is a horn or siren that sounds a warning

explanation.surface: A casino player who is doing badly at last receives a caution.
explanation.walkthrough: A hooter in British English is a car horn or factory siren.
explanation.definitionFit: Craps is a dice game played in Las Vegas casinos, and one who plays it is the answer.

clue.text: Letters from old school hard to get into

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: getting into somewhere means entering it, so one piece slips inside another

parts.note: a gam is a school of whales
H is the pencil grading for hard

explanation.surface: Correspondence from a former school that is difficult to be admitted to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is the group of whales, not a place of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is an early medieval Irish alphabet carved on stones, so it is a set of letters.

clue.text: Young lady going topless — very good!

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top, and in a down answer the top is the first letter

parts.note: slang: 'that was class' means excellent

explanation.surface: An approving remark about a young woman sunbathing without a top.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the top is the first letter, which goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A lass is a girl or young woman, especially in northern English and Scottish speech.

clue.text: Not quiet, little monster making a racket

indicators.note: not tells the solver to leave something out, so the following word's letter is removed

parts.note: a scamp is a mischievous child
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A noisy small child is making a din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' sounds like noise beside 'quiet', but it means a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a dishonest scheme for making money, and so is a scam.

clue.text: Agree to do something about church parking

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps around the pieces that follow

parts.note: to act is to do something
CE is the Church of England
P is the road-sign symbol for parking

clue.text: Approaching fifty-two — surprisingly he doesn't want early retirement

parts.note: nigh means near, approaching

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests something turning out unexpectedly, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

parts.note: L is fifty in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man nearly fifty-two who, oddly, has no wish to retire early from work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early retirement' pretends to be about pensions; it means going to bed early.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stays up late by habit does not want to retire to bed early, the pun on retirement.

clue.text: 'Just like Fox,' describing current politician

indicators.note: describing in its geometric sense means drawing a line round, so one piece encircles the others

parts.note: foxes are proverbially cunning
I is the symbol for electric current
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A quote comparing a current politician to Fox, perhaps the Tory MP Liam Fox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is used in its old sense of drawing round something, so it holds the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Just as an adverb means merely or only, a synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Run at speed covering miles in panicked reaction

indicators.note: a panicked reaction is wild and disordered, so the letters scatter into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for miles

explanation.surface: Animals racing for miles as a frightened response to danger.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer, but 'Run' is the definition and the rest jumbles the letters of 'at speed' around M.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to stampede is to run in a headlong rush, as panicked cattle do.
